transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-17
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chu (Redwood SE), Luca Moreno (Orion Head of Platform), Priya Kapoor (Orion SRE), Darren Cole (Orion ML Engineer)

Summary: high-level scoping session to define a response contract for the POC — what constitutes acceptable performance (time-to-first-response vs per-token speed), how we'll measure p95/p99, sampling plan, and timeline for a 4-week pilot. Discussion included batch behavior, cold vs warm KV cache, and privacy/VPC deployment constraints.

Topics covered: response contract definition, TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, percentile targets (p95/p99), measurement methodology, traffic sampling, dedicated vs hosted fallback, data residency and KMS requirements, next steps and owners.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, uh, and then we'll jump into the response contract framing.
[00:08] Luca: Hey Maya, Luca here. Priya and Darren are on.
[00:11] Priya: Hi, yeah.
[00:13] Darren: Hi all.
[00:15] Ethan: Ethan from Redwood, SE. I'll run through the measurement plan section.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. The goal for this call is to align on acceptance criteria for the POC — what do you need to call it successful? Luca, do you want to start with the business ask.
[00:32] Luca: Sure. So at a high level we want to embed LLM responses into our analytics UI. The main constraints: interactive UI, so first response time matters a lot — customers expect something snappy. But we also have bulk reports where throughput matters. We need both. We're trying to decide whether to set a TTFT (time to first token) SLA or a per-token speed SLA, or both. Also timeline: 4 weeks preferred for pilot.
[00:55] Maya: Great, thanks. Quick definitions so we're aligned: we call TTFT the time from request receipt at the edge to the first token returned to the client; TPOT — and there's some naming inconsistency in the industry — we're using TPOT to mean average per-output-token latency once generation has started, effectively time-per-token across the output distribution.
[01:12] Priya: Got it. Is TPOT the same as tokens per second?
[01:15] Ethan: Related, yeah. If TPOT is 50ms per token then you're doing ~20 tokens/sec, but TPOT captures variability within generation where batching and KV cache affect per-step timing.
[01:25] Darren: We care about p95 and p99 on both measures. For the UI, p95 TTFT < 300ms is ideal, p99 < 800ms is acceptable. For TPOT we want p95 < 40ms, p99 < 120ms — ish. Those are ballpark.
[01:44] Maya: Good candidates. One thing we've seen is that TTFT is dominated by routing, model cold-starts, and prefix cache misses. TPOT is impacted by model size, quantization and batching.
[01:53] Luca: Can you expand on cold vs warm? We have unpredictable query patterns, sometimes the same prefix repeats, sometimes not.
[02:01] Ethan: Yeah so warm cache means KV cache (the attention key-value cache) and other prefix caches are primed by recent requests — that reduces TTFT and improves TPOT because less compute per step. Cold means cache miss, might add 50-200ms overhead depending on kernel and model. For the POC we need to define traffic slices: cold start cases, warm path (repeat queries) and bulk batched jobs.
[02:23] Priya: How should we measure the percentiles? Real production traffic has long tails, do we sample 1% or 10%?
[02:30] Ethan: For the acceptance test we recommend stratified sampling: 72-hour sample broken into: 60% warm interactive traffic, 30% cold/novel prompts, 10% batch long sequences. Minimum sample size 20k requests to get stable p99 estimates — though if your tail is super heavy we might require more.
[02:50] Darren: 20k sounds fine, we'll try to produce a 48–72h sample.
[02:53] Maya: On measurement infra: Redwood will run the benchmark harness against your sample in our test env. Important: the harness respects request timing and simulates concurrency to reproduce realistic batching. We'll ship the harness as a repo link.
[03:05] Luca: Is the harness going to run against your hosted API or Dedicated nodes?
[03:10] Ethan: We can run both. For apples-to-apples we normally run three passes: Hosted (standard instance), Dedicated config that matches the pilot sizing, and a fallback configuration (smaller model/quantized) to show graceful degradation.
[03:22] Priya: About model variants — we have a preferred open model family but we need to know the quantization tradeoffs. How do you report quality regression?
[03:30] Ethan: We'll include a quality bucket with prompt-based checks — a small eval set of 200 golden prompts that we ask your ML team to review for quality thresholds. If quantized model drops below X% pass rate on those checks, we'll flag it as a quality regression and that counts against acceptance.
[03:45] Darren: And how do we align on quality X%?
[03:48] Maya: That's part of the acceptance doc. Many customers use 90–95% on targeted prompts as a starting point, but we'll leave that to you.
[03:55] Luca: Security: we need VPC egress restrictions and KMS for keys, also SOC 2 posture. Is Redwood Private an option for the pilot?
[04:04] Ethan: Yes. Private deployment in your VPC is possible; it adds some setup time (networking and key exchange). For the 4-week pilot we usually do hosted to iterate quickly then pivot to a dedicated/private sandbox in week 2 if you want to stress test network constraints.
[04:19] Priya: That timeline is okay. We prefer PII never leaves our infra so private in week 1 would be better but we can discuss.
[04:26] Maya: Noted. We'll include two variants in the plan: hosted-first and private-first.
[04:31] Luca: Back to SLO numbers — let's make them concrete for the charter we can sign. Proposal: TTFT p95 <= 350ms, TTFT p99 <= 850ms; TPOT p95 <= 45ms, TPOT p99 <= 130ms. These are target acceptance thresholds. Does that look achievable?
[04:48] Ethan: On typical LLMs and modern kernels that seems achievable under dedicated capacity with KV warm paths. Under hosted shared noisy neighbors we may see higher p99. We should add an explicit interference noise budget: e.g., at p99 allow up to +25% penalty during noisy hours but acceptance requires dedicated run results.
[05:04] Priya: Can you explain interference noise budget?
[05:07] Ethan: Sure — if you run on shared hosted endpoints there's variable background load. During the acceptance window we run both dedicated and hosted; dedicated must meet the thresholds. Hosted can be shown for cost comparison but won't be used for acceptance if noisy.
[05:19] Darren: Measurement windows — we want to surface warm vs cold separately in the report.
[05:24] Ethan: Agreed. We'll report p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT across: warm interactive slice, cold interactive slice, and batch slice. We'll also provide aggregated weighted numbers matching your traffic mix.
[05:36] Lucas? [speaker mislabelled as Lucas but we have Luca earlier] Speaker 1: Sorry, small question on telemetry. How granular will traces be?
[05:44] Ethan: We'll provide token-level timestamps and route-level latency breakdowns (edge routing, queueing, model exec, serialization). That is in the console logs. We can also emit an S3 export with per-request rows for analysis.
[05:58] Priya: About the p99 stability — what confidence intervals will you provide?
[06:04] Ethan: We'll run repeated bootstrapped runs and provide 95% CI for p99. That's why we ask for minimum sample sizes.
[06:11] Luca: Ok great. Timeline: can you outline milestones for the 4-week pilot?
[06:16] Maya: High-level: week 0 (this week) — agree contract and traffic sample; week 1 — Redwood sets up harness and baseline hosted runs; week 2 — Dedicated sandbox and private (if requested) deploy and run mixed traffic; week 3 — stress runs and long-tail collection; week 4 — acceptance report and decision. We'll allow a one-week extension if we see heavy tail variance.
[06:36] Priya: That schedule works. Any gotchas we should watch for?
[06:40] Ethan: Yes — payload variance: very long sequences blow up TPOT and throughput. So the harness will re-weight runs to match your production distribution. Also cross-region latency and TLS termination can add to TTFT; include path-specific tests.
[06:55] Darren: For QA, we want a playbook written down: how to reproduce a p99 spike. Is that in scope?
[07:01] Maya: Yes — we'll include a short runbook: how to gather traces, how to replay the request sample, and how to triage model vs infra causes.
[07:10] Luca: Costs — can you provide an estimate of token cost delta between hosted and dedicated?
[07:14] Ethan: We'll provide example unit economics in the follow-up sheet. Dedicated usually reduces per-token cost by 30–60% depending on batch efficiency and quantization. We'll include cost per 1M tokens for both baseline and quantized variants.
[07:26] Priya: A couple of clarifications: 1) If we need end-to-end encryption and HSM, does that add time? 2) Do you support SAML SSO for console?
[07:34] Maya: HSM/KMS adds setup time — typically 1–2 extra business days for key exchange and testing if you're using Redwood Private. SAML SSO is supported for the console and we can configure for your identity provider during week 2.
[07:46] Darren: Also, what happens if the quality guardrails fail? Do we still pass SLOs?
[07:50] Ethan: Quality failures are orthogonal — acceptance requires both perf thresholds and quality thresholds to be met. If perf passes but quality drops below the agreed threshold, the POC is not accepted. We'll show regression dashboards.
[08:02] Priya: Understood.
[08:04] Maya: OK let's capture explicit acceptance criteria for the charter. I'll read what I heard and you correct: 1) TTFT p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 850ms (on dedicated runs). 2) TPOT p95 <= 45ms, p99 <= 130ms (on dedicated runs). 3) Quality pass rate >= 92% on the 200 prompt eval set. 4) Measurement uses a 48–72h traffic sample, min 20k requests, stratified into warm/cold/batch slices. 5) Security: KMS + VPC option available; SOC 2 docs provided. 6) Deliverables: benchmark harness, token-level trace export, acceptance report with CI. Does that capture it?
[08:37] Luca: Yes that looks right. One tweak — can we relax the p99 TPOT to 150ms if sequence lengths > 512 tokens?
[08:44] Ethan: Yes we can add a conditional clause: for sequences >512 tokens allow TPOT p99 <= 150ms. We'll put that in the charter.
[08:52] Priya: Great. Anything else?
[08:55] Maya: Next steps recap: Ethan will prepare measurement plan and harness repo by Friday (2027-02-19). Luca will sanitize and upload the 48–72h traffic sample by Saturday (2027-02-20). Maya will send pilot commercial terms and security package by Thursday (2027-02-18). We'll tentatively schedule the dedicated sandbox demo for 2027-02-24.
[09:12] Darren: Sounds good, thanks.
[09:14] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links.
[09:18] Speaker 2: bye.

--- End ---
